soil-chem-232.title: Reading a sample's elements from its X-rays
soil-chem-232.text: Hit a sample with a beam and it answers in X-rays. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, or EDS, reads that answer to identify the elements present. The beam ejects an inner-shell electron, and when an outer electron fills the hole it releases an X-ray whose energy is characteristic of the element. The beam may be electrons in a microscope or X-rays in an XRF spectrometer. Overlapping peaks and absorption within the sample limit accuracy, so corrections are needed. Wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy resolves finer detail, and newer silicon drift detectors need no liquid nitrogen and work faster.

soil-chem-233.title: Variscite, the green aluminium phosphate
soil-chem-233.text: Variscite is a rare green mineral, a hydrated aluminium phosphate with the formula AlPO4·2H2O. It is a secondary {{ref:soil-found-029}}: it is deposited directly from phosphate-bearing water that has reacted with aluminium-rich rock near the surface. It turns up as fine-grained masses in nodules, cavity fillings and crusts, often alongside veins of crandallite, a calcium aluminium phosphate. The green comes from small amounts of trivalent chromium.

soil-chem-239.title: Why Canadian clays came from the ice
soil-chem-239.text: Most of the layered clay minerals in Canadian soils did not form where they now sit. The continental glaciers delivered them in the parent material. Kaolinite, mica and chlorite come straight from the Canadian Shield, while others in the Interior Plains derive from degraded Cretaceous sediments. Interior Plains clay is mostly smectite, mica, chlorite and some kaolinite. The older Devonian and Silurian sediments of the St. Lawrence Lowlands give mica, chlorite, vermiculite and kaolinite. Little alteration shows across regions. The exceptions are Podzolic and some Brunisolic and Gleysolic soils, where inherited chlorite weathers to expandable {{ref:soil-found-033}}.

soil-chem-241.title: Phosphate minerals and where soil phosphorus goes
soil-chem-241.text: Phosphate forms over 300 minerals. The commonest pure primary ones are the apatites, Ca5(PO4)3(F,Cl,OH), with fluor-, chlor- and hydroxyapatite as the end members. Rock phosphate is mined for fertilizer. Soils typically hold 400-800 mg of phosphorus per kg, against a crustal average of 1050 mg per kg. Phosphate in soil, whether from rock or fertilizer, precipitates with calcium, aluminium and iron. Wet, sub-oxic soils form iron phosphates such as vivianite and strengite. Acidic soils form aluminium phosphate, as in variscite. Calcareous soils form calcium phosphates such as brushite, which commonly precipitates where fertilizer is banded at high concentration.

soil-chem-236.title: Why some minerals vanish from soil faster than others
soil-chem-236.text: A {{ref:soil-form-140}} is not chemically stable at the Earth's surface. During {{ref:soil-found-052}} it dissolves and releases its elements, but at different speeds. Minerals containing sodium and potassium dissolve faster than those with calcium and magnesium, which dissolve faster than those made of silicon, aluminium and iron. Iron depends on conditions: it is soluble as Fe2+ under reducing conditions but forms insoluble Fe3+ oxyhydroxides, like rust, under oxidizing ones. Carbonates precipitate under alkaline conditions and dissolve under acid ones. Carbonic acid from atmospheric CO2 dissolves them, and alkaline deeper groundwater favors precipitation in C horizons.

soil-chem-240.title: Calcite, dolomite and the carbonates in soil
soil-chem-240.text: Where pH falls below 6.0, calcite is not usually found. Soil carbonates are mostly calcite and dolomite inherited from sedimentary rock, with some secondary precipitates in subsurface horizons. Calcite is sparingly soluble, more so at low pH. It dissolves from the upper solum and is redeposited lower as secondary calcite nodules. Dolomite also dissolves from the upper profile, supplying calcium to that calcite while magnesium is mostly leached or taken up by roots. Aragonite is neither common nor stable. Trona, Na2CO3, is highly soluble and found mostly in Solonetzic soils at pH about 9.5. Carbonates keep base saturation, exchangeable Ca and Mg, and pH above 7 high, precipitate phosphate and metals, and stabilize clays and structure. Their entry is {{ref:soil-found-034}}.

soil-chem-242.title: Pyrite, sulfuric acid and gypsum in soil
soil-chem-242.text: Pyrite and other sulfide minerals are absent from well-drained soils. They may occur in poorly drained Gleysolic or Organic soils, tidal soils and mine wastes. Exposed to air, pyrite oxidizes to iron and sulfuric acid: 2FeS2 + 7O2 + 2H2O gives 2Fe2+ + 4H+ + 4SO4 2-. Oxidation of sulfides can push soil pH below 2.0. Mining or excavation that exposes sulfides is mainly responsible for acid rock drainage. Sulfate from sulfide oxidation or other sources forms gypsum, usually at high pH with soluble calcium present.

soil-chem-234.title: Strengite, the purple iron phosphate
soil-chem-234.text: Strengite is a rare orthorhombic iron phosphate, FePO4·2H2O. It resembles {{ref:soil-chem-233}} but is lavender, pink or purple. It is partly soluble, particularly at low pH and low oxidation-reduction potential. The name honors the German mineralogist Johann August Streng. It is another {{ref:soil-found-029}} in which iron, rather than aluminium, holds the phosphate.

soil-chem-227.title: Van der Waals force, the weak pull that adds up
soil-chem-227.text:
No single van der Waals contact is strong, yet fine powders clump because of them. The force is a weak, distance-dependent attraction between atoms or molecules that is not a chemical bond. It begins with a transient shift in electron density that creates a short-lived charge, which a nearby atom is attracted to or repelled by. The force is repulsive at very short range, zero at an equilibrium distance of 0.3 to 0.5 nm for single atoms, and attractive beyond it. Past 1.0 nm it falls off roughly as the 7th power of distance.

Three parts combine: London dispersion forces, Debye forces between permanent and induced dipoles, and Keesom forces between permanent dipoles. Induction and dispersion always attract, while the electrostatic part can attract or repel depending on orientation. Strength rises with polarizability. Pairwise energy is 0.06 kJ/mol between H atoms in H2, 0.44 kJ/mol between O atoms in O2, and 2.35 kJ/mol between xenon atoms.

The forces are additive, cannot be saturated and have no directional character, so many weak contacts can add up to strong attraction. For very small particles, such as fine dry powders, the attraction beats gravity and drag, so the powders are cohesive. Free flow generally needs particles larger than about 250 micrometres. In soils, organic contaminants can be held in organic matter by weak van der Waals interactions, and physisorption is the weak van der Waals form of adsorption. Small particles of the kind met in a {{ref:soil-chem-154}} are where this matters most.

soil-phys-006.title: Flocculation: how clay particles join and drift apart
soil-phys-006.text:
Muddy water that clears in a few hours has usually flocculated. In colloid chemistry, flocculation is when colloidal particles leave suspension as floc or flake. Unlike precipitation, the particles were first merely suspended in a stable dispersion. The IUPAC definition is contact and adhesion that makes larger clusters. This agglomeration is reversible, so the particles can be dispersed again.

In dispersed clay slurries, flocs form once agitation stops, because negative face charges attract positive edge charges. Clay plates flocculate when their slightly positive edges stick to the negative faces of other plates. Sodium displacing polyvalent cations weakens this and deflocculates the clay. The forces involved include van der Waals forces, electrostatic forces and hydrogen bonding.

Flocculation is the opposite of dispersion, in which particles are held apart. The balance between them is set mainly by soil pH, electrical conductivity and sodium content. It also matters for freshwater: highly dispersible colloids make water turbid and adsorb nutrients that drive eutrophication. Floccules become lasting aggregates only once cementing agents stabilize them. The particles involved are the finest of the {{ref:soil-phys-047}}, chiefly {{ref:soil-found-040}} and {{ref:soil-chem-079}}.

soil-chem-225.title: How water plants clear mud with coagulants
soil-chem-225.text: Water treatment borrows the same behavior that clay shows in soil. Coagulation destabilizes charged particles with an added coagulant, and flocculation then gathers them into settleable clusters. Alum is the most common coagulant. Gentle mixing then speeds particle collisions, so destabilized particles enmesh in larger precipitates, depending on mixing shear, intensity, time and pH. A jar test chooses the flocculant and dose by rapid mixing, slow mixing and sedimentation in beakers with paddle mixers. Drinking-water treatment typically runs grates, coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, granular filtration and disinfection. Chitosan is an increasingly popular biodegradable flocculant that binds heavy metals and organic pollutants. See {{ref:soil-phys-006}} and {{ref:soil-chem-154}} for the soil side.

soil-chem-226.title: Muscovite, the common mica
soil-chem-226.text: Muscovite splits into thin, elastic sheets. Also called common mica or potash mica, it is a hydrated phyllosilicate of aluminium and potassium, KAl2(AlSi3O10)(OH)2. Its TOT-c structure stacks tetrahedral-octahedral-tetrahedral layers bonded by potassium cations. Strong bonds within layers and weak ones between them give perfect basal cleavage. It is the most common {{ref:soil-chem-135}}, found in granites, pegmatites, gneisses and schists, and as an alteration product of {{ref:soil-form-141}}. Biotite is almost always much darker. Chlorite is green with inelastic sheets, and pyrophyllite and talc are softer and greasy. Up to 10% of its potassium may be replaced by sodium, and phengite has more silicon than aluminium with Mg or Fe balancing charge. As a {{ref:soil-found-033}} and a {{ref:soil-found-029}}, it is a standard of the group.

soil-chem-228.title: X-ray diffraction and the crystal's hidden order
soil-chem-228.text: A regular array of atoms scatters X-rays as secondary spherical waves. They cancel in most directions but add up in a few specific ones, giving a diffraction pattern. The Bragg model explains these as reflections from evenly spaced sheets in the crystal. Scattering is set by electron density; the heavy nuclei contribute negligibly. Laboratory sources are tubes whose electrons, accelerated through about 50 kV, hit a metal plate. Copper is most common because it cools easily and gives strong K-alpha and K-beta lines, and synchrotrons are far brighter. Where single crystals are unavailable, powder diffraction gives less detailed information. Max von Laue's 1912 observation of diffraction confirmed that X-rays are electromagnetic radiation. Neutrons scatter from nuclei and reveal light atoms such as hydrogen, nearly invisible to X-rays, while electrons scatter 1000 or more times more strongly.

soil-chem-224.title: Dispersion: particles spread through another phase
soil-chem-224.text: Stir mud into water and you make a dispersion. It is a system in which particles of one material are distributed in a continuous phase of another. Dispersions are classed by particle size relative to the continuous phase, whether precipitation occurs and Brownian motion. Particles big enough to sediment make suspensions; smaller ones make colloids and solutions. Dispersing a solid in a liquid separates agglomerated particles and creates a new interface. Molecular diffusion and convection drive it, with convection dominating in turbulent flow and diffusion where there is little turbulence. Above a critical concentration, which depends on particle size and interfacial tension, some liquid dispersions turn into gels or solids.

soil-chem-223.title: Aluminosilicates, the aluminium-silicon backbone of clays
soil-chem-223.text: Aluminosilicates contain anionic Si-O-Al linkages, with cations such as sodium, potassium or hydrogen balancing the charge. They occur as minerals, coal combustion products and synthetic materials, often zeolites, and matter technically as structural materials, catalysts and reagents. {{ref:soil-found-031}} like feldspar are the commonest example: a tectosilicate with potassium, sodium and calcium cations in a negatively charged network of silicon, aluminium and oxygen. Soil alumino-silica clays are aluminosilicates with a regular crystalline or quasi-crystalline structure, including montmorillonite, illite, vermiculite, chlorite and kaolinite. Naturally occurring microporous, hydrous aluminosilicate minerals are {{ref:soil-chem-199}}, whose varying Si/Al ratio tunes their properties. Each is a {{ref:soil-found-029}}.

soil-chem-222.title: Saline, sodic and saline-sodic: three ways soil goes salty
soil-chem-222.text:
Two soils can look equally ruined and need opposite cures. Salt-affected soils are classed as saline, sodic or saline-sodic by total salt (EC) and sodium content (SAR, ESP). Saline soils have EC above 4 dS/m but SAR below 13 and ESP below 15%, with pH usually under 8.5 and flocculated colloids. Sodic soils have EC below 4 dS/m but SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%, and pH usually above 8.5 from hydrolysis of Na2CO3. Saline-sodic soils have EC above 4 dS/m, SAR above 13 and ESP above 15%. Their pH is usually below 8.5 and they stay flocculated.

Sodium explains the difference. Hydrated Na+ between clay particles cancels the binding electrostatic forces, and extra water layers push the particles apart. That disperses sodic soil, and high pH also disperses organic matter. Saline soils stay aggregated with high infiltration, so they leach easily. Dispersed sodic and saline-sodic soils infiltrate poorly and usually need gypsum.

Calcium replacing monovalent Na+ promotes aggregation and infiltration, and the displaced sodium and salts are leached. Saline drainage may be diverted through subsurface drains. Salt-tolerant crops such as barley or sunflower, and trees, can take up salts, but prevention is better than reclamation. Natural sources include mineral weathering, atmospheric deposition, seawater intrusion, saline groundwater and natural brines. Human sources include salty irrigation water, salty fertilizers, manure, biosolids, compost and road salt.

soil-chem-221.title: Two ways to estimate a soil's CEC
soil-chem-221.text: A soil's CEC can be estimated without a full lab run. One way sums the exchangeable cations listed in a soil analysis. The other weights typical values for the clay minerals present. The manual uses 10 cmolc/kg for kaolinite, 100 for montmorillonite/smectite and 150 for vermiculite, though real colloids vary. A soil with 10% kaolinite clay contributes 10 cmolc/kg clay times 10 kg clay per 100 kg soil, or 1.0 cmolc per kg of soil. Colloids, below 0.002 mm, are called the active fraction because their charged surfaces are highly reactive. Their small size gives large surface area per unit weight, and their ionic structure gives a net charge. See {{ref:soil-chem-046}} and {{ref:soil-chem-081}}.
